doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: Ghost writing arrangements for Pee Wee Ellis at CTI
summary: Griffin tells how he ghost wrote CTI arrangements for Pee Wee Ellis, paid by Creed Taylor without credit, and Rowe compares Bucky Pizzarelli's 'Georgia' story.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I bet he got more than $75.

Oh yes. Let me tell you this one, this is a real good one and it’s an honest one. Okay Pee Wee Ellis and I were very good. I was ghost writing for Pee Wee Ellis. So when Pee Wee Ellis would get an arrangement assignment, he lived on Longfellow Avenue in the Bronx. He would call me up. And I didn’t sleep a lot at night. I mean whatever. I slept — I could go two hours sleep for days or nights. So Pee would call me up and it’d be like late at night, so I would go up and he would have these arrangements. “Body Talk” [inaudible] Esther Phillips, and most of those CTI arrangements that you see that Pee Wee Ellis did I was a ghost writer. So we would come up, “Hey Dick, we’ve got to have this ready for tomorrow” and blah. And then he said — he played me the track and he said, “What you hear here?” And I’d start humming. He said, “Write it down.” I would write out the riff and everything. So and then when the recording was done and then the copies and all were made, Pee Wee and I would go down to CTI records and Creed Taylor would call me in and give me a check but no credit on the record or anything of me being on it, see that was the ghost writing. And then he’d call Pee Wee in and pay Pee Wee. And I did that a lot for my ghost writing with Pee Wee.
That is a behind-the-scenes story for sure. © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-

Oh yeah. No one would know who was the ghost writer on a lot of these arrangements. They might have a big name out there, you know this is this person, this is this arranger. But the ghost writing that goes underneath would be much different.

Yes. I remember Bucky Pizzarelli talking about the chart on Ray Charles’ arrangement of “Georgia” and he said, “You know we’re still not sure who actually wrote it.” It’s got someone’s name but he could have farmed it out, it could have been farmed twice or — that’s the music business I guess.
